edges.relationship: The global held to be a human-centred frame, “insufficient (but not unnecessary)” once human history meets geological time, and Big History’s hope that large-scale history yields “global citizenship” questioned (2015–22)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. Tanner Lectures (Yale, 18–19 February 2015; official text read in part, unpaginated), lecture II: "this assumption that thinking on large scales leads to a sense of human solidarity or 'global citizenship' has found a resurgent expression in a branch of historical scholarship that calls itself Big (or sometime Deep) History"; in David Christian's hands "the history of the human species merges seamlessly with the history of 'humanity'"; Christian "directly cites the world-history pioneer William McNeill's 1986 presidential address" (McNeill's words are given only as Christian quotes them). A note on Smail ("I agree, and I do not") announces "Some Friendly Amendments": an amendment, not a rejection. The Review of Politics (2022), his introduction, read in full: the convergence of human and natural histories "has rendered insufficient (but not unnecessary)" the framework of empire, race and global capitalism; labels "such as 'modern' or 'global' now have to be thought together with the much larger-scale units of geological time"; "The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human" (p. 593); his response calls capital and empire "a necessary but insufficient framework" (p. 610). Context: the 2014 Toynbee Prize "for his contributions to global history" (university biography), presented with his lecture "From Globalization to Global Warming" on 3 January 2015 (lecture unread). Reception: Getachew (2022, p. 601) calls the planetary turn "a significant departure from and challenge to" his own anticolonial and postcolonial traditions. edge_124 (post → global, critique) records the group's 2000 critique of Eurocentric global narratives; this is a different, later claim about scale.
edges.map_label: Globe and planet: amending world and Big History, 2015–22

edges.relationship: The distinction between human and natural history, defended “from Hegel and Marx to Croce and Collingwood”, held to collapse under anthropogenic climate change: the starting point of his climate work (2009–22)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. The Review of Politics (2022), introduction, read in full: "This collapse of the distinction, defended over the last two centuries by philosophers ranging from Hegel and Marx to Croce and Collingwood, between humanist histories of humans and their natural histories provides the starting point for my book" (p. 593). The 2009 essay's first thesis (existing reading, p. 201): anthropogenic climate change spells "the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History"; the essay was read in full in an earlier pass (2026-10-14; see its source note), but the passages then recorded (pp. 199, 201, 205–208, 212, 219–222) do not include its discussion of Croce and Collingwood, which was not rechecked in this wave and is not quoted. The edge rests on the 2022 paragraph. Richard Staley (2024, read) summarises the later book's view that postcolonial scholars "inherited a strong human/non-human nature distinction from philosophers of history who argued that history is limited to human affairs" (p. 658), while calling the first thesis "one of the most problematic arguments" of the 2009 essay (see the science critique). This concerns only the human/natural distinction of idealist philosophy of history; it is not the developmental "historicism" ("first in Europe, then elsewhere") that Provincializing Europe criticised (edge_914), a different sense of the word.
edges.map_label: Against the human/natural divide of Croce and Collingwood, 2009–22

edges.relationship: Critics of the four theses question the “species” category, holding inequalities within humanity integral to the ecological crisis (Malm and Hornborg, 2014; abstract only; that they address him is his report), and whether a divide between human and natural history ever existed (the environmental historian LeCain, 2016); Chakrabarty answers that capital is “a necessary but insufficient framework” (2015–22)
edges.evidence_note: Named critics drawn from environmental history, where the 2009 essay was taken up (edge_918). Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg, "The Geology of Mankind?" (Anthropocene Review, 2014): abstract only; it "questions the use of the species category in the Anthropocene narrative and argues that it is analytically flawed, as well as inimical to action", and holds that "Intra-species inequalities are part and parcel of the current ecological crisis". The abstract does not name Chakrabarty; that they "took me to task" is his own report (2016 response, p. 108, existing reading; Tanner lecture I, read, whose note cites them for the "capitalocene" objection). They write as human ecologists, not environmental historians. Timothy LeCain, an environmental historian (Whose Anthropocene?, 2016, existing reading): "it becomes reasonable to ask whether there was ever a divide in the first place" (p. 17). His answers: geological names do not "assign moral responsibility" (Tanner lecture I); "My book does not deny the role of capitalism", capital being "a necessary but insufficient framework" (Review of Politics, 2022, p. 610). Pitts (2022, read) finds his reasons for holding the Capitalocene "at arm's length" in "fascinating and productive" tension (p. 607). Balance from the field: Atte Arffman, reviewing the 2021 book in Environment and History (2022, read), writes that "not many have delved as deep as Chakrabarty does". The endpoint locates named interventions; it does not make them environmental history's verdict.
edges.map_label: Species or capital? Critics of the four theses, 2014–16 (Malm and Hornborg abstract only)

edges.relationship: A historian of science finds the 2009 thesis of a collapsing human/nature divide “one of the most problematic arguments”, since histories of climate such as Golinski’s had stressed the link between human and nature, and the later politics too abstract (Staley, 2024)
edges.evidence_note: One named reader, read in full: Richard Staley, review of One Planet, Many Worlds (British Journal for the History of Science 57:4, 2024): "One of the most problematic arguments of The Climate of History was its assertion that 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History'. This impression of the novelty of the Anthropocene might have been dispelled by attention to the considerable work stressing the common link between human and nature in concepts of climate, such as Jan Golinski's British Weather and the Climate of Enlightenment (2007)" (p. 658); "without engaging in significant emerging literatures on the history and politics of climate science and governance policies, we are left with the somewhat abstract entreaty" (p. 659). Kept in his appraisal: Chakrabarty "has responded to critics and sharpened his account" (p. 657), and the 2023 book is "more appropriately concerned with the recent origins of a separation between humans and nature" (p. 658). Golinski is named only by Staley. The 2023 book is unread. One reviewer, not the field's verdict.
edges.map_label: Staley on the novelty of the divide, 2024

edges.relationship: The Calling of History (2015) reads Jadunath Sarkar’s “imperial liberalism” and his public quarrels with nationalist historians over objectivity and sources, asking when a society values the “cloistered life” of history, as Joshi and the publisher report
edges.evidence_note: The book is unread; its argument is given as its readers state it. Publisher's description: through "more than twelve hundred letters", historians in colonial India "formulated the basic concepts and practices of the field via vigorous—and at times bitter and hurtful—debates in the public sphere". Girija Joshi's review (Práticas da História 3, 2016, read in full): Sarkar appeared "to be a spokesperson for what Chakrabarty calls 'imperial liberalism' (p. 49)", while his rivals of the Bharat Itihas Samshodhak Mandal valued "an ability to understand 'the spirit' of the source" (p. 152); the book asks under what circumstances "a society values the 'objectivity' ... of historical research", and when the public life of history defers to its "cloistered life" (book p. 6; review p. 153). Suman Seth (History and Theory, 2017; abstract only) reads it as "a defense of rationalist history in the face of contemporary threats posed by the rise of a politics of identity in India". A contribution to the history of colonial and national historiography in India; no strand is assigned.
edges.map_label: Jadunath Sarkar and the public life of history, 2015 (as reviewed)

edges.relationship: Historians answer the deconstructive turn she helped bring into Indian history: Eaton names her 1985 reading of Subaltern Studies as a hinge of a turn to “literary criticism” whose costs he finds greater than its gains (2000); Moran rereads the Sirmur records behind her 1985 archive essay and finds the rani “an astute ruler” (2014)
edges.evidence_note: Two named historians without nodes, drawn from the entry for historians' responses to postmodernism (the pattern of edge_257 and edge_933). Richard M. Eaton, "(Re)imag(in)ing Other²ness: A Postmortem for the Postmodern in India" (Journal of World History 11:1, 2000), read pp. 57–61 and 77–78: the collective moved "from a positivist and empiricist orientation to one grounded more squarely in a literary criticism"; in Subaltern Studies IV (1985) "Gayatri Spivak criticized subalternist historians for having adopted positivist methodologies" and, "herself a literary critic, urged historians to continue their efforts to recover subaltern consciousness even while knowing this was impossible" (p. 60); the turn's "modest reminder" is "vastly outweighed" by "an ahistorical and structuralist methodology incapable of explaining historical particularity" (p. 78). His target is the postmodern turn in Indian history as a whole, with Spivak and Cohn as named hinges. Arik Moran, "'The Rani of Sirmur' Revisited" (Modern Asian Studies 49:2, 2015; online 17 September 2014), read in part: "a close reading of the records reveals profound discrepancies between Spivak's interpretation and conditions that existed in and around the kingdom at the time"; the rani "was actually an astute ruler"; her "misreading of evidence goes beyond the boundaries of the discipline as such", although "her fresh approach to source material does point to the cardinal importance of interdisciplinary research". Moran cites Eaton (n. 3). Her 1985 History and Theory essay is unread; its claims are given only as Moran presents them. These are two historians' objections, not the discipline's verdict; in period Prakash and Sarkar read her more favourably (edge_983).
edges.map_label: Eaton and Moran: historians against the reading, 2000–14

edges.relationship: The co-editor of Selected Subaltern Studies (1988) questions Guha’s programme from within: his recovery of subaltern consciousness read as “a strategic use of positivist essentialism” (1985), and his insistence on the “full autonomy” of the subaltern domain not endorsed (1988)
edges.evidence_note: A repair to the pre-2000 core, from existing readings of her own texts. "Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography" (Subaltern Studies IV, 1985; read in full for revision 1.137): quoting Elementary Aspects while "Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain" (p. 341), she reads the project of retrieving subaltern consciousness "as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest" (p. 342). "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988; existing reading of the Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha's autonomous domain, "I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy" (p. 79). Collaboration in the same years: Selected Subaltern Studies (Oxford University Press, 1988), edited by Guha and Spivak (title as recorded on said_subaltern_foreword_1988; Roosa, 2006, n. 4, read). A later historian's summary: Eaton (2000, p. 60) reads the 1985 essay as criticism of "subalternist historians". edge_984 (Spivak → subaltern, critique) carries her critique of the collective's recovery of consciousness and its neglect of gender, and from this revision no longer names the autonomy claim in its relationship; this edge carries the person-to-person disagreement with Guha's autonomy claim, which Guha's own entry already names among the in-period critiques. A critique from a collaborator, not a rejection.

edges.relationship: Hegel’s World-history criticised as a statist, Eurocentric frame, which in Guha’s words as Michael quotes them reached India “as an instrument of the East India Company’s colonial project”, and historians asked to learn from literature the “historicality” of everyday life (2002), as his reviewers and Chakrabarty read the book; Michael finds the argument “mostly confined to the conceptual level”
edges.evidence_note: History at the Limit of World-History (Columbia University Press, 2002) is unread; its argument is given as its readers state it. Bernardo A. Michael (Journal of World History 15:4, 2004, pp. 530–532, read in full): lectures given at the Italian Academy at Columbia; Guha "takes the German philosopher Georg Hegel and his conception of 'World-History' (Weltgeschichte) to task" (p. 530); he quotes Guha that "World-History made its way to the subcontinent as an instrument of the East India Company's colonial project and helped it set up the Raj" (book p. 51) and that history should be "a call for historicality to be rescued from its containment in World-History" (book p. 6). Michael places the book among "recent postcolonial efforts to rethink the practices of disciplinary history and thereby provincialize its European lineages" (p. 532), and objects that "losing sight of the state at the level of the everyday might mean the loss of it as an object of critique", that "Guha's arguments are mostly confined to the conceptual level", and that Guha "seems to attribute to Hegel's World-History an agency that is hard to locate in the historicality of the colonial world" (p. 532). The Company connection is therefore Guha's claim as Michael reports it, and Michael doubts that the book demonstrates how Hegel's ideas became colonial practice. The publisher's description: World-history "reduces the course of human history to the amoral record of states and empires"; historians "should learn from literature"; Tagore's critique of historiography. Chakrabarty (Australian Academy of the Humanities obituary, 2024, read in full) calls it "a grand statement about literature being a far better communicator of senses of the past in the Indian subcontinent than the European discipline of history that had come to India as a practice of the colonial state" and "his farewell to the discipline of history". The theme is older: Chakraborty (2000, read in full) reports that Dominance without Hegemony (1997) already charged colonial historiography with the Hegelian view "that precolonial India had no state, therefore no history" (p. 376). A contribution to the postcolonial critique of historicism alongside Chakrabarty's provincializing argument (edge_914), not a claim that Guha belongs to a school; edge_115 (subaltern → post) records the group.
edges.map_label: Against Hegel’s World-history, 2002 (as reviewers read it)

edges.relationship: Vivek Chibber: Dominance without Hegemony rests on “a highly mythologized story” of the English and French bourgeois revolutions, so its contrast between India’s bourgeoisie and Europe’s fails (2013–14); Sewell and Steinmetz accept the critique of Guha’s Europe, while Chatterjee, as Chibber reports him, denies that Guha made claims about those revolutions
edges.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from comparative historical sociology because his case is a comparison of the European bourgeois revolutions with Indian independence, and because his readers here include historical sociologists (Sewell is already a critic on this roster). Chibber's own words, read in part: Guha's work is "foundational for the entire Subalternist project" and "fundamentally flawed", because its "contrastive claims about the Indian bourgeoisie and Indian capitalism ... rest on a comparison with the European achievement", and "Guha quite dramatically misunderstands the European story" (response to Chatterjee, Verso, 25 February 2014); Guha's break between the bourgeoisies of West and East "flows from a highly mythologized story about the great Bourgeois revolutions, one that was rejected decades ago by historians" (JWSR 20:2, 2014, p. 313). Guha's words appear only as Chibber quotes them (Dominance without Hegemony, p. 19: the bourgeoisie's "historic triumphs in England in 1648 and France in 1789"; p. 5). Readers in the JWSR symposium: William H. Sewell Jr. (pp. 300–303, read in full) calls Guha's portrayal of the two revolutions "standard-issue orthodox Marxism—and ... well past its 'sell-by' date" (p. 301) while finding Chibber's own history "a bit shaky"; George Steinmetz (p. 284) writes that "Guha was relying on a version of Marxist political theory and German history that was demolished by the critics of the Sonderweg thesis"; Bruce Cumings finds the critique "persuasive, at least at the level of how one defines hegemony" (p. 290) but says "I don't know Guha's work" (p. 292), so Chibber's claim that all the critics accepted his reading of Guha (p. 313) is not adopted here. The defence: at the Historical Materialism conference (New York, April 2013) and in a written reply, Partha Chatterjee argued, as Chibber reports him, that Guha made no claims about the classic bourgeois revolutions and criticised only the historiography of colonial India; Chatterjee's text is unread. Chibber's book (Postcolonial Theory and the Specter of Capital, Verso, 2013) is unread; its focus on Guha and Chakrabarty is from Hung's introduction (p. 281). The endpoint locates the intervention; it does not make the critique the field's verdict.
edges.map_label: Chibber’s critique of Dominance without Hegemony, 2013–14

edges.relationship: A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963) traces the Permanent Settlement to the mercantilist, physiocratic and classical political economy of East India Company officials, as Bhambra reads it; she faults its neglect of the colonial context (2024)
edges.evidence_note: A repair to the pre-2000 core. The book (Paris: Mouton, 1963) is unread; it is known through its readers. Gurminder K. Bhambra (Discover Society, 2024, read in full): the book addresses the late-eighteenth-century debates among East India Company administrators over a "permanent settlement", and Guha "set out their different economic premises – deriving from mercantilist, physiocratic, and classical political economy – and demonstrated that, despite their differences, they nonetheless shared a common political focus, establishing the permanence of orderly dominion"; she quotes his p. 9 on entrusting revenue to "a class of native entrepreneurs who had solid interests in the land and were politically reliable". Her criticism: "his failure to locate the discussions of the East India Company administrators within their colonial context". She reports, without these being read here, Sarvepalli Gopal's 1966 view of the book as "primarily ... an exercise in British intellectual history" and Guha's answer in the 1981 preface to the second edition. Holmwood's editorial (2024) calls it "a major contribution to the history of political economy"; Chakrabarty (2024) writes that it "showed an early awareness of the importance of ideas in economic history". A contribution to the history of economic ideas in colonial policy; no claim is made about the book's reception by economists.
edges.map_label: A Rule of Property for Bengal, 1963 (as Bhambra reads it)

edges.relationship: Durkheim’s sociology criticised for taking society as the cause instead of a provisional consequence, against Tarde’s “all things are society”; actor-network theory replaces “the social” with “association” (2002), a programme restated in Reassembling the Social (2005)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. "Gabriel Tarde and the End of the Social", in Patrick Joyce, ed., The Social in Question: New Bearings in History and the Social Sciences (Routledge, 2002), pp. 117–132, read in part in the author's typescript (typescript pp. 1–2, 5, 7, 10): actor-network theory is "a deliberate attempt at terminating the use of the word 'social' in social theory to replace it with the word 'association'", and "ANT actually has a forefather, namely Gabriel Tarde" (p. 1); "Instead of saying, like Durkheim, that we 'should treat social facts as a thing', Tarde says that 'all things are society'" (p. 5); "Durkheim has taken society as the cause instead of seeing that it is never more than a highly provisional consequence" (p. 10). He concedes that he had once "never enquired further than the dismissive footnotes of the Durkheimians" (p. 2). Durkheim's position is given only as Latour presents it. Reassembling the Social (2005) is unread; the author's description presents sociology as "the science of associations and not only as the science of the social". The essay appeared in a volume addressed to historians and social scientists, edited by the historian Patrick Joyce (citation only; Joyce's introduction unread). A critique of Durkheimian sociology, not of the historians who adapted it (durkheim/historical_method).
edges.map_label: Tarde against Durkheim: the end of the social, 2002–05

edges.relationship: An “anthropology of the Moderns”: fieldwork at the heart of modern institutions (science, economy, politics, law) that refuses to believe what the West says about itself, and distinguishes modes of existence that networks alone do not qualify (2012–13)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. An Inquiry into Modes of Existence: An Anthropology of the Moderns (English 2013; French 2012), chapter 1, pp. 27–46, read in full: "LET US IMAGINE AN ANTHROPOLOGIST WHO HAS COME UP WITH THE IDEA OF RECONSTITUTING THE VALUE SYSTEM OF 'WESTERN societies'"; she must "focus on the very heart of modern institutions—science, the economy, politics, law, and so on—rather than on the margins" and resist "OCCIDENTALISM, a form of EXOTICISM applied to what is close at hand, which consists in believing what the West says about itself, whether in praise or criticism" (p. 27); "only a prolonged, in-depth analysis of COURSES OF ACTION" reveals the value system (pp. 27–28); "a contemporary anthropologist has to learn to talk about her subjects of study to her subjects of study" (p. 45). The author's description presents the book as the "positive version" of the question raised by We Have Never Been Modern (1991) and as "a research protocol ... very different from the actor-network theory". Reception here is limited to prize citations: the Holberg committee (2013) names anthropology among the fields his work reached, and the Kyoto citation (2021) credits Laboratory Life with opening an "anthropology of science". No review of the book was read. The reverse arrow, edge_135 (anthropology → latour), records the ethnographic method borrowed for Laboratory Life (1979); this records a later, different claim.

edges.relationship: Latour takes up Chakrabarty’s proposal that the Earth has again become “an agent of history” as a common geostory (2013–14), and answers Chakrabarty’s essay on the planet in a joint conversation on philosophies of history, where Chakrabarty finds much shared ground and offers “friendly amendments” (2020)
edges.evidence_note: In both authors' own words. Latour, "Agency at the Time of the Anthropocene" (New Literary History 45:1, 2014; his Holberg Symposium lecture, Bergen, 4 June 2013), read in full in the author's typescript: "the Earth has now taken back all the characteristics of a full-fledged actor. Indeed, as Dipesh Chakrabarty has proposed, it has become once again an agent of history, or rather, an agent of what I have proposed to call our common geostory" (typescript p. 3; n. 6 cites "The Climate of History: Four Theses", 2009). Latour and Chakrabarty, "Conflicts of Planetary Proportion – A Conversation" (Journal of the Philosophy of History 14:3, 2020), read in part in the authors' typescript: Latour writes in response to Chakrabarty's "The Planet: An Emergent Humanist Category" (2019), calls him "a genuine historian", and writes that "Chakrabarty's introduction of the Planetary triggered a seism in philosophy of history" (pp. 3–4); Chakrabarty answers that "Much of the ground my own thoughts move on is shared with Latour" and offers "friendly amendments" (p. 21); both credit Christophe Bonneuil for the phrase "regimes of planetarity" (n. 50). An acknowledged borrowing and a continuing exchange, not a claim that Latour's later work derives from Chakrabarty; the exchange also runs the other way, and Chakrabarty's environment edge (edge_918) records his own 2009 contribution.
edges.map_label: Chakrabarty’s “agent of history” and Latour’s geostory, 2013–20

'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History', Representations 37 (1992), pp. 1–26, read in full (spacing restored in quotations): 'insofar as the academic discourse of history—that is, “history” as a discourse produced at the institutional site of the university—is concerned, “Europe” remains the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan,” and so on'; '“Indian” history itself is in a position of subalternity'; 'Europe' and 'India' are 'treated here as hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (p. 1). 'That Europe works as a silent referent in historical knowledge itself becomes obvious in a highly ordinary way': 'Third-world historians feel a need to refer to works in European history; historians of Europe do not feel any need to reciprocate' (p. 2). The everyday paradox is that 'we find these theories, in spite of their inherent ignorance of “us,” eminently useful in understanding our societies' (p. 3). 'Let us call this the project of provincializing “Europe”' (p. 20); it 'does not call for a simplistic, out-of-hand rejection of modernity, liberal values, universals, science, reason, grand narratives, totalizing explanations' (p. 20), and 'must realize within itself its own impossibility' (p. 22). Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction pp. 3–23 read in the publisher's excerpt: historicism 'made modernity or capitalism look ... as something that became global over time, by originating in one place (Europe) and then spreading outside it. This “first in Europe, then elsewhere” structure of global historical time was historicist' (p. 7); it 'came to non-European peoples in the nineteenth century as somebody's way of saying “not yet” to somebody else', and Mill's argument 'consigned Indians, Africans, and other “rude” nations to an imaginary waiting room of history' (p. 8). European thought 'is both indispensable and inadequate', and 'this simultaneous indispensability and inadequacy of social science thought is the task this book has set itself' (p. 6); 'provincializing Europe is not a project of rejecting or discarding European thought' (p. 16). The problem of capitalist modernity is 'a problem of translation, as well' as of transition (p. 17). Chapter 1 'reproduces, in an abridged form, a programmatic statement ... that I published in 1992 in the journal Representations' (p. 19). In-period reception and criticism: Arif Dirlik (Critical Inquiry 20, 1994; read) cites the 1992 essay (p. 334, n. 7) for postcolonial criticism's repudiation of the modes-of-production narrative, and objects that 'The denial of capitalism's foundational status also reveals a culturalism in the postcolonialist argument': 'Without capitalism as the foundation for European power and the motive force of its globalization, Eurocentrism would have been just another ethnocentrism' (p. 346). Dirlik's main target is Gyan Prakash; Chakrabarty appears only in his notes (nn. 7, 12). The wider in-period debate, not aimed at him by name: Rosalind O'Hanlon and David Washbrook, 'After Orientalism: Culture, Criticism, and Politics in the Third World', Comparative Studies in Society and History 34:1 (1992), pp. 141–167. The body is closed access; only the publisher's first-page extract and the article's notes (as listed on Cambridge Core) were read. The extract calls Said's blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' in Indian colonial history, directions 'most recently and sharply endorsed in Gyan Prakash's discussion' (p. 141); a note objects that 'Prakash's notion of what constitutes Marxist history is problematic' (n. 13). None of the notes cites Chakrabarty. The 1.132 adversarial review, in a reading not checked here, summarises their case as doubting that the post-foundational programme can sustain historical explanation and political agency, and as holding that Marxist and social historians had already historicised their categories. Prakash replied in the same issue (pp. 168–184). This is criticism of the wider programme, principally Prakash's; it is not evidence of a criticism of Chakrabarty. A contribution, not a founding: the book's epigraph takes 'provincialized' from Gadamer (p. 3), and the post entry already maps Said and Spivak; his argument 'follows directly from my involvement' in Subaltern Studies (p. 15). edge_096 (post → modern) and edge_124 (post → global) stay: they record the group's critiques, which already name him. Later reception, added in revision 1.151 and dated after 2000: the 2007 edition is "Now featuring a new preface in which Chakrabarty responds to his critics" (publisher's page; the preface is unread), and Christopher Hill (Práticas da História, 2020, read in full) reports its claim that globalization was the project's "condition of possibility" (p. 55). Carola Dietze (History and Theory, 2008; abstract only) argues that he "has to be regarded as a thinker of radical historicism rather than as a critic of the discipline of history"; his reply (abstract only) finds "a degree of misapprehension". William H. Sewell Jr. (JWSR, 2014, read in full) writes that "Chakrabarty constructs a 'Marxism' fused with a hyperreal 'Europe' ... and then proceeds to criticize this construct", and "I prefer Chibber's version of the two histories to Chakrabarty's" (p. 302). The symposium divided over this reading: Bruce Cumings (JWSR, 2014, read in part), who says in the same passage that he does not know Guha's work, calls Chibber's account "a preposterous caricature of Chakrabarty's scholarship" (p. 292). Neither reader stands for the symposium as a whole. At the book's twentieth anniversary, Hill finds "ambiguities and contradictions" that are also "the source of its wide impact" (p. 53), and Bo Stråth (read in part) calls it "an immediate success" that "opened up a planetary perspective" (pp. 226, 229).

edge_916.evidence_note: His own statement of the book's aim. Rethinking Working-Class History (1989), preface pp. xi–xv and introduction pp. 3–6, read in the publisher preview (imprint: copyright 1989; first paperback printing 2000; preface dated February 1988): 'In looking at this history in terms of Marx's categories, however, my objective is to develop a critical understanding of these categories themselves'; 'there is an assumption regarding “culture” built into Marx's category of “capital,” and much of what I have to say on Indian labor history, and labor history in general, follows from this reading of Marx' (p. xi); 'this book is an extended polemic against the reductionism' of political-economic analysis of culture, the 'common sense' of Marxist labour history in India; 'Culture, one might say, is the “unthought” of Indian Marxism' (p. xii). 'Perhaps we have long overestimated capitalism's need or capacity to homogenize the cultural conditions necessary for its own reproduction' (p. xiii). He keeps a commitment to equality: 'The struggle to be a “citizen” must be part of the struggle to be a “comrade”' (p. xiv). The figure of the worker in Marx 'was that of a person who belonged to a society where the bourgeois notion of equality was ingrained in culture' (p. 3), and 'there is no “working class” or “working-class consciousness” that ... “is either transcendental in relation to the field of events or runs in its empty sameness throughout the course of history”' (p. 6, quoting Foucault). He separates his argument from Thompson's: 'That my argument is not the same as Thompson's will be clear to any careful reader' (p. 5, n. 9). In-period reception by labour historians: Janaki Nair's review in International Labor and Working-Class History 37 (1990, pp. 96–99; not re-read here; the graph's verification note records that she recognises the theoretical contribution while questioning cultural determination, the treatment of traditions as survivals and the analysis of gender). Rajnarayan Chandavarkar, '“The Making of the Working Class”: E. P. Thompson and Indian History', History Workshop Journal 43 (1997; written for the 1994 History Workshop conference on Thompson; pp. 177–196 read): Thompson's 'inheritance' 'turned in Dipesh Chakrabarty's hands into a static, timeless, indeed Orientalist characterization of a “traditional” Indian, implicitly “Hindu” culture — in Bengal, a predominantly Muslim province' (p. 182); 'Bengali society, indeed Indian society, was now represented as England's proverbial Other' (p. 183); the view 'recently restated by Dipesh Chakrabarty, that rural migrants “imported a peasant culture into the industrial setting”' 'was not the product of an extensive investigation of the nature of labour migration' (pp. 184–185). Sarkar (1997, p. 87, page image checked) praises 'Dipesh Chakrabarty’s stimulating, if controversial, essays on Bengal labour history'; his n. 10 identifies them as the earlier Subaltern Studies essays 'Conditions for Knowledge of Working-Class Conditions: Employers, Government and the Jute-Workers of Calcutta, 1890–1940' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983) and 'Trade Unions in a Hierarchical Culture: The Jute Workers of Calcutta, 1920–50' (Subaltern Studies III, 1984), not the 1989 book. Nair (1990) and Chandavarkar (1997) are the in-period readings of the book itself. In 1992 he wrote that 'My book on working-class history struggles with the problem' of the transition narrative ('Artifice', p. 4). Context, not a genealogy: Eric Hobsbawm is among those he thanks for reading the manuscript (acknowledgments, p. xvii). edge_742 (subaltern → labourhistory) names him and Nair; see the proposed relabel. edge_358 (subaltern → social) stays. Added in revision 1.151, dated later: in a 2020 interview (read in full) he recalls that his Marxist teachers were uneasy at his evidence of Hindu–Muslim conflict among jute workers because, "as readers of E. P. Thompson, they assumed that there was a story waiting to be written about 'the making of the Indian working class'" (pp. 26–27); the paper became "Communal Riots and Labour" (Past and Present 91, 1981; unread). William H. Sewell Jr. (JWSR, 2014, read) reports that Chibber answers the 1989 book by showing that European and American capitalists "have repeatedly relied on personal authority and particularist identities" (p. 301; Chibber's book unread here), and prefers "Chibber's version of the two histories to Chakrabarty's" (p. 302); in the same symposium Bruce Cumings (read in part) calls Chibber's account "a preposterous caricature of Chakrabarty's scholarship" (p. 292), so the symposium did not agree on Chibber's reading.

edge_918.relationship: Climate change and the collapse of the distinction between natural and human history: humans as geological agents, species history and the history of capital (2009), developed into a distinction between globe and planet (2015–22)
edge_918.evidence_note: Dated 2009, after the atlas's 1920–2000 frame: drafted after the user's decision of 2026-10-14 to end the 2000 break. No claim here concerns his work before 2000. 'The Climate of History: Four Theses', Critical Inquiry 35, no. 2 (Winter 2009), pp. 197–222, read in full. The first thesis: 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History' (p. 201). His readings in 'globalization, Marxist analysis of capital, subaltern studies, and postcolonial criticism ... had not really prepared me for making sense of this planetary conjuncture' (p. 199). On environmental history: 'the rise of environmental history in the late twentieth century made the breach wider', but 'environmental history, where it was not straightforwardly cultural, social, or economic history, looked upon human beings as biological agents', quoting Crosby's preface to The Columbian Exchange (p. 205); 'Scholars writing on the current climate-change crisis are indeed saying something significantly different from what environmental historians have said so far ... Humans now wield a geological force' (p. 206); the distinction between human and natural histories, 'much of which had been preserved even in environmental histories that saw the two entities in interaction—has begun to collapse' (p. 207). 'The mansion of modern freedoms stands on an ever-expanding base of fossil-fuel use' (p. 208). 'A critique that is only a critique of capital is not sufficient' (p. 212), yet 'the story of capital ... cannot be denied by recourse to the idea of species' (p. 219); the task is 'to mix together the immiscible chronologies of capital and species history' (p. 220). He ends with a 'negative universal history' (p. 222). Reception after 2009, labelled by date: Robert Emmett and Thomas Lekan, eds., Whose Anthropocene? Revisiting Dipesh Chakrabarty's 'Four Theses' (RCC Perspectives 2016/2, from a February 2015 workshop; read in part): the essay 'has become a primary text for understanding the problematic nature of the Anthropocene as a cultural category' (p. 7) and challenges 'ecological histories that situate humans as biological agents' (p. 8). The environmental historian Timothy J. LeCain (2016) writes, tentatively, that the theses 'may prove more radical than even he intended, or perhaps desires' (p. 15). Criticism: in his 2016 response Chakrabarty concedes to Carol Boggs that 'one can no longer separate the biological agency of humans from their geological agency in the way in which I appeared to do' (p. 104), and reports that 'Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg took me to task' over 'There are no lifeboats for the rich', quoting Kathleen McAfee: 'Contra Chakrabarty, the rich may face the same storms and they do have lifeboats' (p. 108). Malm and Hornborg (2014) are known here through their abstract, which holds that "Intra-species inequalities are part and parcel of the current ecological crisis", and through his reports; the body of their article is unread. A contribution that disputes the field's prior framing of human agency, not a founding claim for climate history. Later work, added in revision 1.151: the Tanner Lectures (2015, read in part) distinguish humanity as "homo" from the scientists' "anthropos" and conclude that "we have fallen into 'deep' history"; The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021; publisher's page and contents; unread) is summarised in his own words: "The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human" (Review of Politics, 2022, p. 593). In environmental history's own journal, Atte Arffman (Environment and History, 2022, read) writes that "historians can no longer dismiss material realities and non-human world" and that "not many have delved as deep as Chakrabarty does". The criticisms of the species category and of the divide's novelty are now drawn separately (environment → Chakrabarty; science → Chakrabarty).

edge_983.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988), read in the Williams and Chrisman reprint (pages of that reprint; its opening is abridged): ‘Some of the most radical criticism coming out of the West today is the result of an interested desire to conserve the subject of the West, or the West as Subject’ (p. 66). ‘Two senses of representation are being run together: representation as “speaking for”, as in politics, and representation as “re-presentation”, as in art or philosophy’; ‘representing them, the intellectuals represent themselves as transparent’ (p. 70); running vertreten and darstellen together ‘leads to an essentialist, utopian politics’ (p. 71). The codification of Hindu law is her ‘example of epistemic violence’ (pp. 76–77), and she asks whether, ‘inside and outside the circuit of the epistemic violence of imperialist law and education’, ‘can the subaltern speak?’ (p. 78). On sati she sets the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, which she says she ‘put together’ (p. 92), against ‘the Indian nativist argument’, ‘“The women actually wanted to die”’: ‘The two sentences go a long way to legitimize each other. One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness’ (p. 93). She qualifies: ‘Given that the abolition of sati was in itself admirable’ (p. 94); ‘Obviously I am not advocating the killing of widows’ (p. 97). ‘Between patriarchy and imperialism, subject-constitution and object-formation, the figure of the woman disappears ... into a violent shuttling’ (p. 102). She welcomes ‘all the information retrieval in these silenced areas’ in history and other disciplines, while warning that the assumed ‘consciousness or subject’ will ‘cohere with the work of imperialist subject-constitution’ (p. 90). The close: ‘The subaltern cannot speak. There is no virtue in global laundry lists with “woman” as a pious item. Representation has not withered away’ (reprint p. 104, wording restored from the unpaginated 1988 text in Morris, 2010; 1988 p. 308 per Sunder Rajan in the same volume). She credits Lata Mani’s 1983 thesis on sati as ‘a brilliant account’ and ‘profited from discussion with Ms Mani’ (n. 65, p. 109). The 1999 revision (A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, ch. 3; read in Morris’s unpaginated reprint; CPR p. 308 per Sunder Rajan) says: ‘in the first version of this text, I wrote, in the accents of passionate lament: the subaltern cannot speak! It was an inadvisable remark’, and that Bhubaneswari Bhaduri ‘was not a “true” subaltern’. ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (Critical Inquiry, 1985, read pp. 243–245) opens: ‘It should not be possible to read nineteenth-century British literature without remembering that imperialism, understood as England’s social mission, was a crucial part of the cultural representation of England to the English’, and finds it ‘particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism’ (p. 243). In-period readings by historians: Gyan Prakash, ‘Can the “Subaltern” Ride?’ (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint 2000, pp. 226–227, read): ‘as Spivak states starkly, the debate left no room for the woman’s enunciatory position’; ‘Spivak very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman as the point at which the interpreter must acknowledge the limits of historical understanding’. Sumit Sarkar, ‘Orientalism Revisited’ (Oxford Literary Review, 1994; reprint p. 254, n. 14, read), criticising Mani’s Saidian assumptions, contrasts ‘the much more substantive discussion of pre-colonial and colonial discourses on sati in Spivak’. Contested in period: Terry Eagleton (LRB, 13 May 1999; web text, no page numbers, read) on A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ to be the critique its title promises, ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’, yet ‘this study boldly addresses the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’; he reports that she contrasts her own critique with Aijaz Ahmad’s ‘scorching assault’ in In Theory (1992; unread here). Benita Parry, ‘Problems in Current Theories of Colonial Discourse’, Oxford Literary Review 9 (1987), pp. 27–58, is the best-known in-period critique; it is closed access and unread, and no claim is made about its argument. A contribution, not a founding: the post entry already lists Said (1978) before her, and edge_107 (language → post) and edge_115 (subaltern → post) stay. Later reception, added in revision 1.151: Interventions 4:2 (2002) devoted a special issue to A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, from a panel at the IAPL conference in 2000, with her response (metadata and abstracts only); Mark Sanders's abstract holds that placing "Can the subaltern speak?" in the book's "History" chapter "emphasizes its deconstruction of Marxist politics". Ritu Birla's abstract (the essay is unread) explores "the challenges of radical history writing" through the book's chapter on history, under the themes of "limits, the open secret, and value/transvaluation"; it sets Spivak beside Joan Scott's critique of "experience", opening "a discussion of the supplementary relationship of literature and history", and connects the limit of history to "the selective production of the archive".

edge_984.relationship: A critique from within: the collective's recovery of subaltern consciousness read as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', and woman shown to be 'the neglected syntagm' of its accounts of insurgency (1985–88); the subaltern later reformulated as those 'removed from lines of social mobility' (2004)
edge_984.map_label: Strategic essentialism and the gendered subaltern, 1985–2004
edge_984.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’, Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363, read in full: the group ‘offers a theory of change’, plotting change ‘as confrontations rather than transition’ (p. 330); its practice is ‘closer to deconstruction’ than its self-description (p. 332); ‘This is why I hope to align them with deconstruction’ (p. 336). ‘Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain’ (p. 341), she reads the project to retrieve subaltern consciousness ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’ (p. 342), which ‘would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness’ (p. 356). On gender: ‘The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women’, but ‘I think they overlook how important the concept-metaphor woman is to the functioning of their discourse’ (p. 356); ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357); ‘Male subaltern and historian are here united in the common assumption that the procreative sex is a species apart’ (p. 358); ‘woman is the neglected syntagm of the semiosis of subalternity of insurgency’ (p. 359); ‘if the question of female subaltern consciousness ... is a red herring, the question of subaltern consciousness as such must be judged a red herring as well’ (p. 360). She qualifies: ‘The making-visible of the figure of woman is perhaps not a task that the group should fairly be asked to perform’, but ‘a feminist historian of the subaltern must raise the question of woman as a structural rather than marginal issue’ (p. 361). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha’s ‘autonomous domain’, ‘I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy’ (p. 79; this disagreement with Guha is drawn as its own person-to-person critique, Spivak → Guha, in this revision, and is no longer named in this edge's relationship); ‘the colonized subaltern subject is irretrievably heterogeneous’ (p. 79); ‘If, in the context of colonial production, the subaltern has no history and cannot speak, the subaltern as female is even more deeply in shadow’ (pp. 82–83). In-period readings from historians of the field: Rosalind O’Hanlon, ‘Recovering the Subject’ (Modern Asian Studies, 1988; Verso reprint, read), takes up her phrase (p. 80, citing SS IV p. 342) but warns ‘we should certainly hesitate before accepting Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s suggestion that the strategy of the Subaltern series “in claiming a positive subject-position for the subaltern might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times”’ (p. 105, citing SS IV p. 345). Gyanendra Pandey, a member, reads the 1988 close as Gramsci’s point: ‘“The subaltern cannot speak,” writes Gayatri Spivak, making, I suggest, much the same point’ (Ethnos, 1995; reprint p. 285, read). Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that the 1988 essay ‘brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies’ and ‘may have provided a major impetus’ for the gender and voice themes of Subaltern Studies IX (1996). Her own later account (‘The New Subaltern’, 2000, read): ‘Except in the work of Susie Tharu ... Subaltern Studies is not informed by feminist theory as such’ (p. 325), and of 1985, ‘Subaltern Studies had no need of such apologetics. But the theoretically inclined metropolitan identitarians did’ (p. 332). Later reading, labelled: Partha Chatterjee (2010; Morris volume, unpaginated) recalls first reading both essays in 1985 with ‘bewilderment’ and calls her intervention ‘the poststructuralist moment in Subaltern Studies’, adding that a changed political context also drove the shift. A critique from within, not a rejection: she joined the editorial collective in the 1990s. edge_389 (gender → subaltern) carries the same story under the gender entry; see the proposed relabel. Guha’s person edge (pe137_guha_rel_01, guha draft) cites the same 1985 essay as reception; this edge is hers. Later reformulation and reading, added in revision 1.151 and dated after 2000: in "Righting Wrongs" (South Atlantic Quarterly, 2004; read in part, from a February 2001 lecture) she writes, "By subaltern I mean those removed from lines of social mobility" (p. 531), and warns that leaders from the domestic "below" ignore "the historically established discontinuity between themselves and the subaltern" (p. 535). Richard M. Eaton (Journal of World History, 2000, read p. 60) summarises the 1985 essay as criticism of "subalternist historians" for "positivist methodologies" (see the truthdebate critique).

Laboratory ethnography is a specified contribution, not Latour’s creation of all STS. Revision 1.151 adds two later judgements, attributed as such: Andrew Pickering (Modernism/modernity, 1994, read in full) called Science in Action (1987) "the most important book on science, technology and their intertwining with society published in the 1980s", whose actor-network analysis "flew in the face of technological and social determinist perspectives" (p. 257); the Holberg committee (2013) wrote that he "completely re-imagined Science Studies, pioneering new ethnographic methods" and that his work of the 1980s "established Actor Network Theory (ANT) as a widely used methodology". rationale: The four entries stopped at 2009 (Chakrabarty, one point after 2000), 1999 (Spivak), 1989 (Guha) and 1999 (Latour), with two to four chronology points each. Every new edge rests on the person’s own words or a named reader’s explicit statement, read in full or in part with pages; abstract-only, metadata-only and prize-citation readings are labelled, and unread books are attributed locally to their reviewers. No new edge repeats an existing endpoint/type combination; later work that would have duplicated an arrow (Chakrabarty → environment; Spivak → subaltern) goes into edge revisions instead. Named critics without nodes are drawn through group entries with the critic named in the text (Chibber via historicalsociology; Malm, Hornborg and LeCain via environment; Staley via science; Eaton and Moran via truthdebate). Six edge revisions are made without retargeting: edge_914, edge_916 and edge_918 (Chakrabarty), edge_983 and edge_984 (Spivak), and edge_134 (Latour → sts). Three people records are added (vivek_chibber, richard_m_eaton, arik_moran). An Indigenous-history critique arrow for Ackerly, a Spivak → subaltern contribution parallel to edge_984, and Latour arrows to environment and historicism are left out (see release/README.md).

text_revisions.old: A historian of modern South Asia in the Subaltern Studies collective. He argues that, within university-based historical discourse, an imagined 'Europe' remains its dominant theoretical reference: 'the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan”', where 'Europe' and 'India' are 'hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (1992). text_revisions.old: A literary theorist and the translator of Derrida’s Of Grammatology (1976), whose essays on colonial India became reference points for historians. In ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ (1985) she read the collective ‘from within but against the grain’, proposing that its recovery of subaltern consciousness be read ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’, and argued that it overlooked ‘how important the concept-metaphor woman is’ to its own discourse. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988) separates representation as ‘speaking for’ from ‘re-presentation’, argues that in Foucault and Deleuze’s conversation intellectuals, ‘representing them, ... represent themselves as transparent’, and reads the British abolition of sati through the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, set against the nativist ‘The women actually wanted to die’: between them ‘One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness.’ She later called the essay’s closing ‘the subaltern cannot speak!’ ‘an inadvisable remark’ (1999). In period, Gyan Prakash (1992) held that she ‘very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman’ as a limit of historical understanding, Rosalind O’Hanlon (1988) urged hesitation ‘before accepting’ her proposal to re-inscribe the series’ strategy ‘as a strategy for our times’, and Terry Eagleton (1999), crediting the book with addressing ‘the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’, found her Critique ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ and ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’.

text_revisions.old: A historian of colonial India, who taught at Sussex and the Australian National University and edited Subaltern Studies from its first volume (1982) until he left the editorial team in 1988. The opening statement holds that the historiography of Indian nationalism 'has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism', and that it leaves out 'the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain' that 'neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', while allowing 'a great deal of overlap' between the two (1982). Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983) attributes 'a consciousness' to the rebel peasant, holds that Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India', and reads that consciousness through the records of counter-insurgency; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (1983) finds colonial, nationalist and radical histories alike making the rebel 'only a contingent element in another history with another subject'. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989; book 1997) defines hegemony, against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony', as dominance in which 'Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)', and argues that colonial dominance had 'quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony'. In period, Spivak (1985) read the recovery of subaltern consciousness as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', O'Hanlon (1988) found 'the classic figure of Western humanism' readmitted 'in the figure of the subaltern himself', Bayly (1988) found that the approach sometimes seemed to postulate an 'unchanging peasantry', and Sarkar (1997) an 'unnoticed drift' towards nationalist positions 'even in Guha's initial formulation of the project'.

After 2000, History at the Limit of World-History (2002), lectures given at Columbia’s Italian Academy, takes Hegel’s World-history to task as a statist frame and asks historians to learn from literature the “historicality” of everyday life, in its reviewers’ accounts; Guha’s claim, as Bernardo Michael quotes it, is that World-History reached India “as an instrument of the East India Company’s colonial project”. Michael welcomed the turn to everyday life but warned that “losing sight of the state ... might mean the loss of it as an object of critique”; he also found the argument “mostly confined to the conceptual level”, without showing how Hegel’s ideas became colonial practice (2004). Dipesh Chakrabarty later called the book “his farewell to the discipline of history”, after which Guha wrote in Bengali (2024). Vivek Chibber’s Postcolonial Theory and the Specter of Capital (2013) made Dominance without Hegemony a central target, arguing that its contrast between Indian and European bourgeoisies rests on “a highly mythologized story about the great Bourgeois revolutions”; William Sewell agreed that Guha’s portrayal of the English and French revolutions was “standard-issue orthodox Marxism”, while Partha Chatterjee, as Chibber reports him, denied that Guha made claims about those revolutions at all (2013–14).

text_revisions.new: Studies the practical work through which scientific claims become established facts, including experiments, inscriptions, instruments, and relations among researchers. Laboratory ethnography offers a route into science studies that should not be collapsed into textual interpretation or into Bloor’s programme. The Pasteur study extends his inquiry into historical scientific change and distinguishes that analysis from an explanation by social forces alone. Bloor’s 1999 response contests the treatment of sociological explanation in the Pasteur case. Law’s 1986 edited volume provides a particular publication context shared with Callon; collaboration does not establish agreement. Andrew Pickering called Science in Action (1987) “the most important book on science, technology and their intertwining with society published in the 1980s”, read We Have Never Been Modern (1991; English 1993) as an account of a modern constitution that purifies nature from society, and objected that it leaves no room for the specific histories of labour, gender, colonialism and empire (1994). After 2000 he turned against Durkheim, presenting Gabriel Tarde as the forefather of actor-network theory in a volume on new bearings in history and the social sciences (2002). In “Why Has Critique Run out of Steam?” (2004) he asked whether he had been wrong “to participate in the invention of this field known as science studies”, while refusing “to swear that I will never be a constructivist any more”. His published description of Reassembling the Social (2005) presents sociology as “the science of associations and not only as the science of the social”. In An Inquiry into Modes of Existence (2012; English 2013) he imagined an anthropologist who studies the Moderns’ own institutions while refusing to believe “what the West says about itself”. Politics of Nature (1999; English 2004) proposed new institutions for political ecology; reviewing it, Antony Puddephatt found original propositions despite “an overall lack of empirical rigor” (2004). In his Holberg lecture (2013) he took up Dipesh Chakrabarty’s proposal that the Earth has again become “an agent of history” and called it a common geostory; the two discussed philosophies of history in a joint conversation (2020). By his own published descriptions, Facing Gaia (2015; English 2017) uses Lovelock’s Gaia to “disentangle the ethical, political, theological, and scientific aspects of the now obsolete notion of Nature”, and Down to Earth (2017; English 2018) defines politics “as what leads toward the Earth and not toward the global or the national”. The Holberg committee wrote that his influence reached “history, art history, philosophy, anthropology, geography, theology, literature and legal studies” (2013); he received the Kyoto Prize in 2021. Science in Action, We Have Never Been Modern, Politics of Nature, Reassembling the Social, Facing Gaia and Down to Earth are unread here; their arguments are given as reviewers, the prize committees or his own published descriptions state them. No review of An Inquiry into Modes of Existence, Facing Gaia or Down to Earth was read, so the debates around his later work are not covered here.

field_sets.value: The earlier parts of this entry rest on the readings recorded in its source notes. Revision 1.151 adds readings made on 2026-10-19: “Gabriel Tarde and the End of the Social” (2002) in part, in the author's typescript; chapter 1 of An Inquiry into Modes of Existence (2013) in full; “Agency at the Time of the Anthropocene” (2014) in full, in the author's typescript; the 2020 conversation with Chakrabarty in part; Pickering's (1994) and Puddephatt's (2004) reviews in full; and the Holberg (2013) and Kyoto (2021) citations. “Why Has Critique Run out of Steam?” (2004) is an existing reading. Science in Action, We Have Never Been Modern, Politics of Nature, Reassembling the Social, Facing Gaia and Down to Earth are unread; they are known through reviewers, the prize citations and his own published descriptions. No review of An Inquiry into Modes of Existence, Facing Gaia or Down to Earth was read, so the reception of his later work, including debates over his climate politics, is not covered here. The prize citations are the prize bodies' judgements, not historians' reception. He is not presented as the sole founder of science studies.
